projects.name: nikaVSimulator
projects.label: V
desc: An in-browser simulator for the Tang Nano 9K FPGA. Write Verilog in a Monaco editor, run it through a sandboxed Icarus Verilog backend, and watch the board’s pins and waveforms come alive without touching real hardware.
The simulation backend runs untrusted HDL inside locked-down, network-less containers on a rootless Podman socket — full isolation from the host even if the input is hostile.
highlights: Live board pin overlay synced to the simulated waveform.
Ephemeral, fully sandboxed per-run containers — no network, dropped capabilities, resource caps.
Deployed self-host, embeddable cross-origin by other tools.

projects.name: STM Simulator
projects.label: S
desc: A simulator for the STM32 "Blue Pill" that lets bare-metal C firmware be tested without the physical board in hand — faster iteration, and CI that doesn’t need hardware in the loop.
Compiles and runs firmware through a sandboxed QEMU backend, then renders the resulting GPIO/peripheral trace on a live board view.
highlights: Models core peripherals closely enough to run real firmware.
Turns "flash and pray" into a tight edit-run loop.
Useful when hardware is shared or unavailable.

projects.name: SA Grid NILM
projects.label: N
desc: Research into Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM): disaggregating the power draw of individual household appliances from a single, whole-house smart-meter signal — no per-device sensors required.
The work is tuned for the South African context, where load-shedding and an unstable grid break many of the assumptions baked into NILM datasets from elsewhere.
highlights: Built a preprocessing pipeline robust to grid interruptions and missing windows.
Compared classical event detection against sequence models for disaggregation.
Framed accuracy around the appliances that matter for demand-side management.

projects.name: CubitEdge
projects.label: C
desc: A self-hosted DevOps platform that bundles git hosting, CI runners and a container registry into a single, deployable stack — so a small team can own its whole pipeline.
Born from wanting to understand my toolchain end-to-end instead of stitching together someone else’s black boxes.
highlights: One-command deploy of git + CI + container registry.
Feasibility study weighing Forgejo against building from scratch.

projects.name: Egg Theory
projects.label: E
desc: An action-RPG side project — a playground for gameplay systems, combat feel and the kind of design problems that have nothing to do with my engineering coursework.
A reminder that I’m drawn to ideas broadly; the restlessness across domains is part of the point.
highlights: Designed the core combat loop and enemy behaviours.
Hand-tuned game feel: hit-stop, knockback, timing windows.
Built as a deliberate break from hardware work.

projects.name: Signal Gen
projects.label: G
desc: A programmable signal generator taken from requirements through CAD and firmware — a full-stack hardware project from schematic capture to a working board.
highlights: Requirements capture, schematic and PCB layout.
Firmware for waveform synthesis and control.
End-to-end ownership from spec to bring-up.

posts.title: Getting the 'why' right before the build
pars: It’s tempting to start building the moment a problem is handed to you. The tools are right there, the deadline is real, and typing feels like progress. I’ve learned to resist that pull.

Before I reach for a tool, I try to understand the fundamentals of what I’m actually solving. Getting the why right — why this approach, why this constraint matters, why the obvious solution fails — saves far more time than moving fast ever does.
It also means giving myself room to be wrong early, when being wrong is cheap. A wrong assumption caught on paper costs an afternoon. The same assumption caught in silicon costs a semester.

posts.title: What NILM taught me about noisy signals
pars: Non-intrusive load monitoring asks a deceptively simple question: given one aggregate power signal for a whole house, can you tell which appliances are running?

The hard part isn’t the model. It’s that the real signal is a mess — overlapping loads, sensor noise, and a grid that, in South Africa, is anything but steady. Load-shedding turns your clean training distribution into a rumour.
The lesson that stuck: spend your effort understanding the signal before you tune the model. Most of my accuracy gains came from framing the problem, not from a fancier network.

posts.title: Notes on self-hosting my whole toolchain
pars: I wanted my git hosting, CI and container registry to live on hardware I control. CubitEdge started as that itch — one deployable stack instead of five SaaS logins.
Self-hosting teaches you how the tools you take for granted actually fit together. You stop seeing "CI" as a magic button and start seeing runners, queues and caches.
Is it more work? Sometimes. But I understand my pipeline now in a way I never did when it was someone else’s black box.
